newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy centre-right says may help govt on sell-offs.
newsitem.headline: Italy centre-right says may help govt on sell-offs.

text.p: Opposition centre-right parties said on Sunday they might help Prime Minister Romano Prodi push through his ambitious privatisation programme in a bid to beat dogged resistance to the plans from a hardline government ally.

Prodi appealed at the weekend for cross party support for the planned sale of a raft of major state companies after the Communist Refoundation, which secures the government's parliamentary majority, promised to fight the proposals.
The prime minister's call was immediately answered by Pierferdinando Casini, leader of the small centrist CCD party which lies within Silvio Berlusconi's Freedom Alliance bloc.

"We do not plan to become an escort for this government but on certain policies which reflect those of our party, our vote won't be lacking," Casini told a CCD rally. "On privatisations, for example, we will vote in favour, if asked to."
But Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti warned Prodi against accepting help from the centre-right. "It would be suicide for the government," he told reporters.
U.S. investment bank J.P. Morgan has estimated that European privatisations could total a record $53 billion in 1997, with up to $20 billion of this coming from Italy alone.
Top of the Italian sales list is telecommunication giant Stet, with further shares in motorway group Autostrade and energy conglomerate ENI also due to hit the market later this year.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told reporters on Saturday that the centre-left government was committed to placing all state holdings in private hands, despite delays in getting the necessary legislation through parliament.
"The Treasury will be happy the day when it can call a news conference to say that it has sold everything," he said.
That day may be far off unless Prodi can find a way around Communist Refoundation's ideological opposition to the sale of firms in key strategic areas, such as telecommunications.
Prodi's centre-left "Olive Tree" coalition has no outright majority in the lower house of parliament and has to rely on Refoundation's 35 deputies to pass legislation.

The Marxist party demonstrated its power last week by abstaining in a lower house vote to transfer a controlling interest in Stet from state holding IRI to the Treasury as a prelude to Stet's privatisation. Prodi lost the motion.
"On specific points the government has to count on wider support. One of these points is privatisation," Prodi said at the weekend.

Media magnate Berlusconi gave a lukewarm reception to the call for help, but hardright leader Gianfranco Fini suggested that his party, traditionally seen as opposed to sell-offs, might now be ready to vote for the privatisations.
However Prodi's eight-month-old government will need outside backing for more than just the state disposals.

His coalition has recently embarked on a review of the welfare state in the face of growing calls from economic bodies to cut generous pension handouts. Before the findings are even released, Refoundation is already making its postion clear.

"Certainly if the government follows the path of privatisations and also puts the welfare state in question, it will be shifting towards the right, and certainly we will head for a crisis," Bertinotti said.
